newsitem.title: FRANCE: Arthuis urges political body to counterbalance ECB.
newsitem.headline: Arthuis urges political body to counterbalance ECB.

text.p: Europe must give itself the political means to counterbalance the power of the future European Central Bank through an informal council of ministers, French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said in an interview published on Monday.
He also said the launch of the new single currency, the euro, combined with this "stability council", would give Europe greater weight to push for a stronger dollar.

The European Commission had estimated, he said, that the exchange rate between the dollar and the european currency unit (Ecu) over recent years had cost Europe more than one percentage point in growth.

"With the euro, and the stability council, our desire for a rising dollar will be listened to more. It is indeed one of the reasons for a single currency," he said in an interview with financial daily La Tribune Desfosses.

Arthuis, who attended a meeting of European Union finance ministers in Dublin this weekend, said that France's call for a stability council had been welcomed favourably by Germany, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, among others.
"From January 1, 1999, there will be a powerful central monetary power in the European Central Bank. Where will be the necessary political counterbalance?" he said.
"That will be the role of a stability council, where the finance mininsters in the euro zone will meet on an informal basis," he said.

France's proposal for a stability council did not appear to win a particularly enthusiastic reception at the Dublin talks, but nor was it rejected out of hand at a meeting which already had too heavy an agenda to look in detail at new proposals.

Arthuis repeated France's desire for sanctions against countries which let their currencies swing sharply against the euro and which did not join the new exchange rate mechanism to be launched for countries not yet ready to join monetary union.
"We are supported by some countries, even though there is no unanimity on the part of the 15 (EU members) on the subject.
"I would like us to have concrete proposals on excessive currency fluctuations before the Amsterdam summit (of EU leaders) in June 1997," he said.

France's original proposals, that the EU pay aid to member countries in their national currencies rather than Ecus -- thereby penalising them for any devaluation -- have already been rejected as unworkable by the European Commission.
